{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791668968001,"t":"edit","title":"Basecamp","text":"{{Infobox tool | name = Logos Basecamp | what = Desktop app that runs the Logos stack on your own machine | licence = MIT and Apache 2.0 | code = https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp | use = https://docs.logos.co/basecamp/install-logos-basecamp | build = https://docs.logos.co/basecamp/install-logos-basecamp#build-and-run-logos-basecamp-from-source | verified_on = 9 October 2026 | verified_against = GitHub release 0.3.2 and the install docs }} '''Logos Basecamp''' is the desktop app for [[Logos]]. It bundles a blockchain node, a wallet, a module manager and other tools in one install. The docs call it the default launcher for the stack. It starts the Logos runtime on your computer, loads a set of modules and gives them one interface. == What it does == The Basecamp page on logos.co lists these features: * '''Wallet.''' Accounts on the Logos Execution Zone. Send and receive tokens, including private transfers that use zero-knowledge proofs. * '''Private messaging.''' Encrypted peer-to-peer chat over the Logos messaging layer, with no central relay. * '''Blockchain explorer.''' Browse blocks, transactions and activity on the Logos Execution Zone. * '''File sharing.''' Decentralised storage, with the file index kept on your device. * '''Node dashboard.''' Run a full blockchain node and take part in the [[Testnet]]. * '''Package manager.''' Browse, install and update modules. The page says Basecamp needs no accounts, sends no data to third parties and has no cloud dependencies. The Testnet v0.3 release added a Monero wallet and Ethereum wallet apps. == Platforms == Prebuilt installers are published for: * macOS on Apple silicon (.dmg) * Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit Intel or AMD (-x86_64-setup.exe) * Linux, 64-bit Intel or AMD (-x86_64.AppImage) * Linux on ARM64 (-aarch64.AppImage) WSL2 on Windows is also supported. The docs ask for 4 GB of RAM (8 GB recommended) and about 2 GB of free disk space. Not every app runs on native Windows yet. Chat and Storage do. The blockchain node and the swap app need the Linux AppImage under WSL2. == Install it == # Go to the [https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp/releases/latest latest release] and download the file for your system. # '''macOS:''' open the .dmg and drag Basecamp into Applications. # '''Linux or WSL:''' install the few system libraries the docs list, make the AppImage executable and run it. # '''Windows:''' run the setup file. It does not need administrator rights. The installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen may warn you. Choose "Install (recommended)" or a portable copy. The [https://docs.logos.co/basecamp/install-logos-basecamp install guide] has the exact commands, a build-from-source route with Nix, and fixes for common errors. == Latest release == The latest release on GitHub is '''0.3.2''', published on 6 October 2026. Its notes cover: * optional packages offered during installation * reinstalled apps that open without a restart * fixes to how the package catalogue shows installed packages * more accurate CPU figures in the module inspector * the storage module pinned to 3.0.2 Earlier release tags in the repository: {| class="wikitable" ! Version !! Tag date |- | 0.3.2 || 6 October 2026 |- | 0.3.1 || 1 October 2026 |- | 0.3.0 || 22 September 2026 |- | 0.2.3 || 4 August 2026 |- | 0.2.2 || 29 July 2026 |} The 0.3.0 notes include a Windows installer with a portable mode, an uninstall option in the App Manager, app-to-app intents and download progress bars. == See also == * [[Run a node]] * [[Testnet]] * [[Getting started]] * [[Logos]] * [[Tools]] == Sources == * [https://logos.co/basecamp Logos Basecamp], logos.co, read 9 October 2026 * [https://docs.logos.co/basecamp/install-logos-basecamp Install Logos Basecamp], Logos documentation, Testnet v0.3 * [https://docs.logos.co/get-started/what-is-logos What is Logos?], Logos documentation * [https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp/releases/tag/0.3.2 Logos Basecamp 0.3.2 release], GitHub, 6 October 2026 * [https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp/releases Logos Basecamp releases], GitHub, read 9 October 2026 * [https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp Logos Basecamp repository] (licence files and tags), GitHub * [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v03-release Testnet version 0.3: release notes], Logos roadmap {{Page status|Usable}} [[Category:Logos]]","summary":"Parallel Wiki build: page from sourced research, source-checked 9 October 2026","as":"Eleutherious"}

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791668968002,"t":"edit","title":"Booth","text":"{{Infobox tool | name = Booth | what = A broadcaster module for Basecamp that announces your live stream over Logos Messaging | stage = Prototype | licence = MIT or Apache-2.0 (your choice) | code = https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp | use = https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp#install-into-logos-basecamp | build = https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp#build | verified_on = 9 October 2026 | verified_against = README and release v0.2.4 (5 October 2026) }} '''Booth''' is a module for [[Basecamp]] that turns your computer into a broadcast station, with no platform, account or directory server behind it. == What it does == * You point OBS at Booth and press Start. Booth runs a MediaMTX origin and announces your station over Logos Messaging topics. * Booth only broadcasts. Listening happens in a separate module, the Receiver. * A station is its public key. Booth signs every announce with that key, so nobody can take over your station by copying its name. * Each signed station gets a three-word fingerprint made from its key. Tell your listeners the three words so they can check it is really you. * You pick an identity tier. Anonymous sends unsigned announces. Autogenerated keeps a key on this one machine. Keycard keeps the key on a Logos Keycard, so the same identity works on any device with the card. * You pick who can find you. A public station appears in the directory every Receiver watches. Since v0.2.2, a private station announces on a topic made from its title and a passphrase, and the announce is encrypted. * You pick how much of your address shows. "Hide IP with Tor" runs a Tor hidden service and announces a .onion address. "Show IP (LAN)" is a direct pull for local, low-latency use. * A station re-announces every 15 seconds and drops off a Receiver's list 45 seconds after the heartbeats stop. Stage: Prototype. The README opens with "This is a personal, experimental hobby project." It also says Booth is not an official Logos product and is not audited. == Use it == # Install Logos Basecamp v0.2 or later. The signed releases are built for Linux (amd64). # Install the runtime tools: OBS Studio, MediaMTX, ffmpeg and tor. The .lgx packages do not bundle them. From v0.2.1 a first-launch card lists anything missing and gives you the install command. # Download both packages from the [https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp/releases releases page]: radio_module and radio_ui. Install both with lgpm. The internal module names stay radio_module and radio_ui after the rename to Booth. # Booth needs the delivery module. On Basecamp 0.3.x the package manager installs it as a dependency. The README says the old pin to delivery v0.1.1 only matters on a Basecamp 0.2-era host. # Open Booth in Basecamp. Name the station, pick identity, reach and privacy, then press Start. # Copy the ingest values from the OBS setup card into OBS (WHIP, RTMP or SRT) and start streaming. When the light shows Live, the station is signed and announced. Guides in the repository: [https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp/blob/main/docs/CONNECTING-OBS.md Connecting OBS] and [https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp/blob/main/docs/ZERO-TO-STREAMING.md Zero to Streaming], an end-to-end guide for a headless station. == Build it == * Booth builds with Nix. Build the core with cd radio_module && nix build, then launch the UI with cd ../radio_ui && nix run .. * ./scripts/install.sh builds both .lgx packages and installs them into Basecamp. * Headless tests for the core and the UI are listed in the README. * Ports, the directory topic, the heartbeat and the time-out can be changed with RADIO_* environment variables. == Releases == * v0.1.0, 10 June 2026: first release. * v0.2.2, 28 July 2026: private streams. * v0.2.3, 13 August 2026: network fix for the logos.test preset. * v0.2.4, 5 October 2026: makes stations visible again on Basecamp 0.3.x. This is the latest release. == User reviews == Add your review on the [[Talk:Booth|talk page]]. == See also == * [[Issue 1/Radio Basecamp]], the LAN Issue 1 article on Booth and the history of pirate radio * [[Basecamp]] * [[Tools]] == Sources == * [https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp booth-basecamp README], GitHub, updated 5 October 2026 * [https://github.com/xAlisher/booth-basecamp/releases booth-basecamp releases], GitHub, v0.1.0 to v0.2.4 * LAN Issue 1, "Radio Basecamp", page 26, September 2026 (see [[Issue 1/Radio Basecamp]]) {{Page status|Usable}}","summary":"Parallel Wiki build: page from sourced research, source-checked 9 October 2026","as":"Eleutherious"}

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791668976001,"t":"edit","title":"Charter 77","text":"'''Charter 77''' was an informal civic initiative in Communist Czechoslovakia. It took its name from a declaration published in January 1977. The declaration asked the state to respect the human rights it had already signed up to. The initiative ran until 1992. [[Václav Benda]] wrote "[[The Parallel Polis]]" in 1978 as a discussion paper for its spokespeople and signatories.

== What it was ==
=== The trigger ===
In 1976 the authorities broke up a festival of the underground "second culture" and arrested members of the rock band The Plastic People of the Universe and people around them. They were tried and convicted of "organised disturbance of the peace". The sentences ran from eight to eighteen months. The case showed that the regime would punish independent culture as well as open political dissent. It brought together the people who went on to write the Charter. In 2003 the Supreme Court of the Czech Republic overturned the 1976 verdicts.

=== The declaration ===
The first preparatory meeting took place on 10 December 1976 in the Prague flat of Jaroslav Kořán. Signatures were collected on individual cards. The founders included Václav Havel, Jan Patočka, Jiří Hájek, Zdeněk Mlynář, Jiří Němec, Ladislav Hejdánek, Pavel Kohout, Ladislav Lis, Martin Palouš and Václav Benda.

The text was dated 1 January 1977. It said the government had failed to honour rights set out in the 1960 Constitution, the 1975 Helsinki Final Act and the 1966 UN covenants on civil, political, economic and cultural rights. Those covenants had taken effect in Czechoslovakia in March 1976. The declaration called the signatories a "loose, informal, and open association of people". It said the Charter did not form the basis for any oppositional political activity. This wording kept it within a law that banned organised opposition.

On 6 January 1977 Havel, Ludvík Vaculík and Pavel Landovský tried to deliver the text to the Federal Assembly and the government. Police detained them and confiscated the original. On 7 January it appeared in western newspapers including Le Monde, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung and The Times. English Wikipedia dates its appearance in The New York Times to 27 January. Radio Free Europe and Voice of America broadcast it back into Czechoslovakia. At home it circulated only as [[Samizdat]]. The state never published it.

=== Signatories ===
The first 242 signatories came from many occupations, political views and religions. About 1,200 people had signed by the mid-1980s. Nearly 1,900 had signed by January 1990. Only 25 publicly withdrew their signatures. Well-known signatories included Václav Havel, Jan Patočka, Jiří Hájek, Pavel Kohout, Ludvík Vaculík, Marta Kubišová, Jaroslav Seifert, Jiří Dienstbier, Petr Pithart and Václav Benda.

=== The state's response ===
The Communist Party daily ''Rudé právo'' attacked the signatories in an article titled "Losers and usurpers". Officials organised a counter-declaration, the "Anticharter". It was signed by 76 National Artists, 360 Meritorious Artists and more than 7,000 other artists. Many signed under pressure, out of fear or without knowing the text of the Charter.

Signatories lost their jobs. Their children were refused education. Some were forced into exile or stripped of citizenship. Others were tried and imprisoned. Jan Patočka, one of the first spokespeople, died on 13 March 1977 after long police interrogations.

== How it worked ==
Charter 77 had no members, no presidium and no programme. One of its first signatories called it "a very loose platform", a breeding ground for opposition activity.

* '''Spokespeople.''' The first three were Václav Havel, Jan Patočka and Jiří Hájek. The rotation was not in the original declaration and developed over time. Each year a trio of spokespeople was named. They were chosen to cover as wide a range of views as possible, and they were often the most persecuted signatories. More than 40 people served in all. The spokespeople vouched that documents issued in the Charter's name were genuine. Václav Benda served from 1 February 1978, and again from 1 January 1984 to early 1985.
* '''Documents.''' Between 1977 and 1989 the Charter issued 598 documents. They covered political trials, censorship, police abuse and other rights violations.
* '''VONS.''' In April 1978 signatories founded the Committee for the Defence of the Unjustly Persecuted (VONS) to publicise the fate of people associated with the Charter. In October 1979 six VONS members, Havel and Benda among them, were tried for subversion and jailed.
* '''Reach.''' Most signatories lived in Prague. Most citizens knew of the Charter mainly through the state's campaign against it.

In 1984 Charter 77 received the first Andrei Sakharov Freedom Award. After November 1989 its members helped negotiate the transfer of power, and Havel became President of Czechoslovakia. On 3 November 1992, after the fall of the Communist regime, the spokespeople met in Prague and formally ended the Charter's work.

== Why it matters to Logos ==
Benda wrote "[[The Parallel Polis]]" in 1978 as a discussion paper for Charter 77's spokespeople and signatories. On 12 June 2025 Logos held a Circles meetup in Brno to discuss that essay. The event page says "the need for parallel societies lives on". Logos calls itself "the private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies".

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669256000,"t":"edit","title":"Commitment pooling","text":"'''Commitment pooling''' is a practice in which a community turns its members' promises of goods and services into vouchers and places them in shared pools, so people can exchange what they are able to offer.

== The basics ==
Grassroots Economics describes commitment pooling as "A protocol and practice for routing promises, settlement, and mutual support through shared pools." In its docs, "communities issue redeemable commitments as Community Asset Vouchers, place them in shared pools."

The Grassroots Economics glossary defines a voucher as "A promise denominated in an agreed upon Unit of Account". The voucher is issued and accepted in exchange for money or in kind.

Will Ruddick set out the idea in "Letters from the Field: Commitment Pooling, An Economic Protocol Inspired by Ancestral Wisdom". The paper appeared in the ''International Journal of Community Currency Research'' (volume 27, pages 54 to 79) on 30 June 2023. Its abstract describes "pooling of commitments, as a mechanism for curating and fairly exchanging resources" within communities. It links the protocol to traditional mutual service practices.

Grassroots Economics calls itself "a community of practitioners, stewards, engineers, educators, researchers". Its docs say the service formerly presented as Sarafu Network has moved to Cosmo-Local Credit (CLC).

== How it applies to Logos ==
No Logos source yet.

== Examples ==
* '''Binguni and Mbele, Kenya.''' A Grassroots Economics case study describes a rural region of 400 households facing chronic money scarcity. Binguni, a self-organised savings group, pooled commitments of seeds, water, cooking and labour. Mbele's women farmers joined later with erosion control and water management. One member committed 10kg of seeds worth 2,500 KES. The Binguni group capped issuance at 50,000 BIGIs and agreed a 2% monthly decay to encourage flow.
* '''Sarafu, Kenya.''' A paper in ''Scientific Data'' (2022) by Carolina E.S. Mattsson, Teodoro Criscione and William O. Ruddick describes Sarafu as a "digital complementary currency in Kenya". It began as local physical community currencies and moved to a feature-phone interface in 2017. One Sarafu is worth roughly one Kenyan shilling. From 25 January 2020 to 15 June 2021 the data covers about 55,000 users and transactions totalling around 300 million Sarafu. Savings and lending groups called chamas are central to the system.
* '''Sarafu Network on Celo.''' The Grassroots Economics website reports 26,367 users, 285,197 peer-to-peer exchanges, 188 active commitment pools and 745 active vouchers, for 5 July 2023 to 20 July 2025.

== Background ==
Petty holds a PhD in chemical physics and a BSc in physics, both from Texas Tech University. He began researching blockchains around 2012 as a hobby during his PhD. He later worked in data science and in security for industrial control (ICS/SCADA) networks. Earlier employers include Booz Allen Hamilton and Novetta. He became Chief Security Officer at Status in January 2020.

He co-founded The Bitcoin Podcast Network. He co-hosts ''Hashing It Out'', a technical podcast on decentralised technology. Past guests include Vitalik Buterin and Dan Boneh.

== The Transaction Supply Chain ==
His LAN article is [[Issue 1/Transaction Supply Chain]]. Logos has published a related article, "PriFi and the Incomplete Institution: Securing the Transaction Supply Chain" (15 September 2026). It argues that blockchains protect settlement well but leave the other stages of a transaction exposed, from discovery and negotiation to enforcement. See [[PriFi]].

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669260000,"t":"edit","title":"Cypherpunk","text":"A '''cypherpunk''' is someone who promotes strong cryptography and privacy-enhancing technology as a way to bring about social and political change.

== The basics ==
Eric Hughes, Timothy C. May and John Gilmore founded the cypherpunk group in late 1992. It met monthly at Gilmore's company, Cygnus Solutions, in the San Francisco Bay Area. Jude Milhon coined the name at an early meeting, blending "cipher" and "cyberpunk".

The Cypherpunks mailing list began in 1992. It had about 700 subscribers by 1994, and an estimated 2,000 by 1997. Wikipedia describes the movement as libertarian in outlook, valuing decentralisation and individual autonomy.

Two texts set out the ideas:
* '''"A Cypherpunk's Manifesto"''' by Eric Hughes, dated 9 March 1993. It opens: "Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age." It argues that "privacy in an open society requires anonymous transaction systems." It warns that "We cannot expect governments, corporations, or other large, faceless organizations to grant us privacy". Its answer is to build the tools: "Cypherpunks write code."
* '''"The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto"''' by Timothy C. May, dated 22 November 1992. It begins: "A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy." May also wrote ''The Cyphernomicon'' (1994), a cypherpunk FAQ.

== How it applies to Logos ==
The Logos manifesto, by Jarrad Hope, says the project "traces its origins to the founding ideals of the cypherpunk movement." It states: "Privacy is not secrecy, it is a fundamental right."

The Logos homepage describes private-by-default technology "to reclaim civil society". The Logos blog published a podcast episode, "Peter Ludlow: Crypto Anarchy and Cyberstates", on 31 January 2024.

== Examples ==
Projects and people Wikipedia links to the movement:
* PGP, created by Philip Zimmermann. Hal Finney was the main author of PGP 2.0.
* Bitcoin, invented under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto.
* Tor, which enables anonymous web browsing.
* Hashcash, invented by Adam Back.
* b-money, a cryptocurrency proposal by Wei Dai.
* WikiLeaks, founded by Julian Assange, who joined the mailing list around 1993 to 1994.

'''DeFlock''' is an open-source project that maps automatic licence plate readers (ALPRs) across the United States, so people can see where they are being tracked.

== What it does ==
* It shows ALPRs on a map, with their type and the direction they face. The locations come from OpenStreetMap and are added by volunteers.
* It explains how to report a camera with a standard set of OpenStreetMap tags.
* It keeps a growing guide to ALPR makes and models, with photos, so you can recognise them.
* Its stated aim is to raise awareness of ALPRs and help the public push for accountability and privacy protections.

The old address deflock.me now redirects to deflock.org.

== Who runs it ==
* William Freeman created the project and holds the copyright on the code. In the README he writes that he started it after noticing mass deployment of ALPRs.
* The code is under the MIT licence on GitHub, in the FoggedLens organisation.
* The site lists local groups fighting mass surveillance. It says they are run independently and are not affiliated with DeFlock.

== Join or copy it ==
* Get the DeFlock app for [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/deflock-me/id6752760780 iOS] or [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=me.deflock.deflockapp Android], or use the OpenStreetMap iD editor in a browser.
* Adding or editing map data needs a free OpenStreetMap account. An email address is enough to sign up.
* Find a local group on the [https://deflock.org/groups Local Groups] page.
* Copy or improve the code: [https://github.com/FoggedLens/deflock website], [https://github.com/FoggedLens/deflock-app app] and [https://github.com/FoggedLens/deflockhopper_maps map].

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669264000,"t":"edit","title":"Exit","text":"'''Exit''' is leaving a system that is failing you, rather than staying to change it from within.

== The basics ==
The term comes from the economist Albert O. Hirschman's book ''Exit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States'' (Harvard University Press, 1970).

Hirschman argued that when a firm, organisation or state declines, its members have two responses. They can leave, which he called '''exit'''. Or they can complain and push for change, which he called '''voice'''. Exit only signals that something is wrong. Voice can also show why. His general principle is that the easier exit is, the less likely people are to use voice.

'''Loyalty''' changes the sums. Loyal members may hold back from leaving. They tend to invest more in an organisation when they believe their voice will be heard.

Critics have argued that exit and voice can work together, that the model overlooks problems of collective action, and that loyalty can produce silence.

=== In crypto and parallel-society writing ===
At Y Combinator's Startup School in 2013, Balaji Srinivasan, whom Reason called a startup veteran, applied the same framework to countries. Reason reported his summary as "you can try voice or you can try exit." In a country, voice means voting and exit classically means emigration. Srinivasan also described exit more broadly as tools that let people "peacefully opt out" of bad policy without entering politics. He said "Exit amplifies voice", because visible departures draw attention. He predicted that 3D printing, Bitcoin and telepresence would make exit easier. Reason noted that his framework echoes Hirschman.

== How it applies to Logos ==
The Circles handbook's "What is Logos?" page says: "All people should be free to exit hostile, corrupt, and inefficient systems."

The Logos manifesto, by Jarrad Hope, uses Hirschman's three terms. It calls for "a culture of resilient parallel societies" that raises the costs of surveillance and coercion while "minimising the costs of exit, voice, and loyalty." It also says: "If you do not agree with what you have consented to, you are always free to leave or remix."

The Logos homepage says "Basecamp is the tool for living outside existing systems." See [[Basecamp]].

== Examples ==
* East Germany, 1989. Mass emigration led people who stayed to protest in the streets. Wikipedia sums up Hirschman's later reading: "Exit triggered voice, and both worked in tandem."
* Latin American exile. Hirschman described rulers who encouraged critics to leave the country as using exit as a safety valve.
* State schools. When quality-conscious parents move their children to private schools, the voices best able to diagnose a school's decline leave with them.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669266000,"t":"edit","title":"FAQ","text":"Questions newcomers ask about [[Logos]], answered from official sources. Each answer links to the page with more detail.

== About Logos ==
=== What is Logos? ===
Logos is a social movement and a decentralised technology stack. The stack has blockchain, storage and messaging layers, joined by a runtime called Logos Core. The movement organises local groups called Circles. See [[Logos]].

=== Who runs the λPrize? ===
The Logos Collective Association, registered in Switzerland, administers the λPrize. It sets the prizes, judges the claims and pays the winners. See [[λPrize]].

== Circles ==
=== What is a Circle? ===
A Circle is a self-organised local group that meets in person at least once a month. Each Circle works on a [[Winnable issue|winnable issue]], such as a clean-up, a campaign or a fundraiser. See [[Circles]].

=== Do I need a background in tech to join? ===
No. The Circles handbook says you do not need a particular background. What counts is caring about building something real with others. See [[Getting started]].

=== How do I start a Circle? ===
Fill in the Circle Steward form at [https://logos.co/activist-leader-steward logos.co/activist-leader-steward]. Logos reviews each proposal and replies. The [https://circles.logos.co/ Circles handbook] covers how to prepare and run the first meeting.

== Software and nodes ==
=== What is Basecamp? ===
Basecamp is the Logos desktop app. It bundles a node, a wallet, private chat, file sharing and a package manager. It runs on macOS (Apple silicon), Windows and Linux. See [[Basecamp]].

=== Can I run a node on Windows? ===
Use WSL2. The full-node guide assumes a Linux host, and the command-line blockchain guide covers Linux, macOS on Apple silicon and Raspberry Pi 5. On Windows, Basecamp runs the blockchain node through the Linux AppImage under WSL2. See [[Run a node]].

=== What computer do I need to run a node? ===
The docs ask for 2 CPU cores at 2 GHz, 1 GB of RAM and 1 to 2 GB of free SSD space. On x86_64 the CPU must support the ADX instruction. A full node also needs a public IPv4 address and several open ports. See [[Run a node]].

=== How do I get testnet tokens? ===
Since Testnet v0.3, new participants can earn testnet tokens by proof-of-work mining, without waiting for anyone to approve a request. Your node starts mining once it is online and you run the start command. See [[Run a node]] and [[Testnet]].

=== Which testnet version is current? ===
Testnet v0.3, announced on 30 September 2026. Its blockchain module 0.3.1 starts a new chain, so nodes must start from an empty state. See [[Testnet]].

== Building ==
=== What is the difference between a λPrize and an RFP? ===
A λPrize is claimed after the work is built and in use, by opening a solution pull request. An RFP is a grant you apply for with a proposal before you start, run in milestones. See [[λPrize]] and [[RFPs]].

=== What licence must my code use? ===
λPrize submissions must be dual licensed under MIT and Apache 2.0. RFP work must also be open source under MIT and Apache 2.0, unless Logos agrees otherwise.

=== How are λPrizes paid? ===
In USDT on Ethereum, after your solution is merged. You give your legal name, country and an Ethereum address. The address is public, so a single-use address is suggested. See [[λPrize]].

=== Can Logos staff or contractors win a λPrize? ===
No. Logos service providers and their contractors may not take part. They are also not counted when judging adoption. See [[λPrize]].

=== How long does an RFP review take? ===
Logos reviews proposals weekly and usually replies within 14 days. A grant only exists once a Grant Agreement is signed. See [[RFPs]].

=== Where do builders ask questions? ===
On the Logos Discord, in the #builder-hub channel. The Logos Forum is used for longer discussion. Questions about an RFP can go on your proposal issue on GitHub.

=== What still needs building? ===
See [[Still to build]] for open prizes and RFPs.

'''FundBrave''' is a decentralised fundraising platform built by people in the Logos movement. [[Circles/Benin City|Logos Circle / Benin City]] used it to raise money for the medical care of a member's parents in 2026.

== What it does ==
* Donors can give in naira by bank transfer, or in USDC, ETH or DAI sent straight to a vault.
* The campaign page offers "Stake & Earn": a donor stakes USDC in Aave V3 on Base, keeps the principal and shares the yield with the campaign.
* The campaign page says every transaction is logged on-chain and lists no platform fees.
* The README describes a wider design: social features, staking pools, optional anonymous donations and AI tools. It lists deployments on several EVM networks, including Polygon, Base, Celo and Arbitrum.

=== The Benin City campaign ===
* At the May 2026 meetup, Logos Circle / Benin City heard that both parents of a member were seriously ill. The Circle opened a campaign on FundBrave for the family.
* The crypto sits in a multisig. Moving it takes three of five signers, and three keys are held inside the Circle and the family. Each release is tied to a named treatment.
* By 27 May 2026 the Circle had raised over ₦750,000 of a ₦1.5 million goal.
* The campaign did not reach its final goal. On 22 July 2026 the Circle reported the mother's surgery a success.

== Who runs it ==
* FundBrave was presented at the Benin City Circle's meetup on 7 February 2026. The report described it as a "decentralized fundraising platform" combining social features with DeFi yield.
* LAN Issue 1 says its founder is a Logos Regional Steward. The founder called the Benin City campaign "the most meaningful proof of the idea so far."
* The February report named two open problems: onboarding people new to crypto wallets, and security where social features meet money.

== Join or copy it ==
* See a live campaign at [https://benin.fundbrave.com benin.fundbrave.com].
* The code is on [https://github.com/FundBrave/FundBrave GitHub] under the MIT licence. It is a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js frontend, a NestJS backend, Solidity contracts and a Python AI service. The README has a quick start that needs Node.js 18, Python 3.11, PostgreSQL and Redis.
* The repository's contributing guide points newcomers to issues labelled "help wanted" and "difficulty:easy".
* A Circle can copy the model from Benin City: a public campaign, a multisig with keys split between the Circle and the family, and each payout tied to a named need.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669270000,"t":"edit","title":"Getting started","text":"This page lists the ways to take part in [[Logos]]. Pick one. Each line points to a wiki page or to the official source.

== Try the software ==
* '''Install Basecamp.''' Basecamp is the Logos desktop app. It bundles a node, a wallet, chat, file sharing and a module manager. See [[Basecamp]] or download the [https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp/releases/latest latest release].

== Run a node ==
* '''Run a node.''' Node operators help decentralise and secure the network. The official guide is at [https://docs.logos.co/run-a-node docs.logos.co/run-a-node]. See [[Run a node]] for a summary.
* '''Sign up for the node programme.''' Logos takes early-access sign-ups for an upcoming node programme at [https://logos.co/node-programme logos.co/node-programme].

== Organise locally ==
* '''Join a Circle.''' Circles are local groups that meet in person at least once a month and work on a local problem. Find one in the [[Circles]] directory, on the [https://logos.co/movement#circles-map movement map], or follow [https://circles.logos.co/readme/about-logos-circles/how-to-join-a-logos-circle How to join a Logos Circle].
* '''Start a Circle.''' If there is no Circle near you, propose one through the [https://logos.co/activist-leader-steward Circle Steward form]. Logos reviews each proposal and replies. The [https://circles.logos.co/readme/for-circle-stewards Circles handbook for Stewards] explains how to run the first meeting.

== Build ==
* '''Win a λPrize.''' λPrizes pay for working, adopted software on the Logos stack. Claims are made by pull request. See [[λPrize]] or the [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize prize repository].
* '''Answer an RFP.''' RFPs are grants for a set piece of work, paid against milestones. You apply with a proposal. See [[RFPs]] or the [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp RFP repository].
* '''Read the docs and examples.''' Start with the [https://docs.logos.co/ documentation], the [https://github.com/logos-co/scaffold Scaffold boilerplate] for LEZ programs, and the sample apps for [https://github.com/logos-co/eth-lez-atomic-swaps atomic swaps] and [https://github.com/logos-co/lez-multisig multisig].
* '''Browse community ideas.''' The [https://github.com/logos-co/ideas Logos Community Idea Board] collects project ideas from the community.
* '''See what is missing.''' [[Still to build]] lists open prizes and RFPs in one place.

== Become an Activist Builder ==
* '''Apply as an Activist Builder.''' Activist Builders turn community needs into tools, systems, research, media and infrastructure. Apply at [https://logos.co/activist-builder logos.co/activist-builder]. See [[Activist Builder]].

== Write ==
* '''Read LAN.''' See [[LAN]] and [[Issue 1]].

== Talk to people ==
* '''Forum.''' Circle reports, prize and RFP announcements and tech news are posted on the [https://forum.logos.co/ Logos Forum].
* '''Discord.''' The [https://discord.gg/Ykv4eZyHUJ Logos Discord] is the main community hub. Builders meet in the #builder-hub channel.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669272000,"t":"edit","title":"Glossary","text":"Every term on this wiki, A to Z. Format from Moneropedia.

== A ==
; Activist Builder
: Someone who turns community needs into "working tools, systems, research, media, and infrastructure", in the words of the Logos Activist Builder page. See [[Activist Builder]].

== B ==
; Basecamp
: Logos Basecamp, "a self-contained desktop application" for running a full Logos node, managing a wallet and installing modules. See [[Basecamp]].
; Blend
: The part of the Logos Blockchain that propagates transactions and blocks privately. See [[PriFi]].

== C ==
; Chama
: A savings and lending group in Kenya. Chamas are central to the Sarafu system. See [[Commitment pooling]].
; Charter 77
: An informal civic initiative in Czechoslovakia whose declaration was published on 6 January 1977. It criticised the government for failing to implement human rights commitments. See [[Charter 77]].
; Circle
: A Logos Circle, one of the "self-organised groups solving winnable issues that matter locally". See [[Circles]].
; Commitment pooling
: A protocol and practice in which communities issue redeemable commitments as vouchers and place them in shared pools. See [[Commitment pooling]].
; Community Asset Voucher
: A redeemable commitment issued by a community and placed in a shared pool, in the Grassroots Economics model. See [[Commitment pooling]].
; Cosmo-Local Credit
: The service that Sarafu Network moved to, according to the Grassroots Economics docs. See [[Sarafu Network]].
; Cryptarchia
: The private proof-of-stake consensus of the Logos Blockchain. See [[PriFi]].
; Crypto anarchy
: The idea set out in Timothy C. May's "The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto" (22 November 1992). See [[Cypherpunk]].
; Cypherpunk
: Someone who promotes strong cryptography and privacy-enhancing technology to bring about social and political change. See [[Cypherpunk]].

== E ==
; Exit
: Leaving a failing system rather than staying to change it. The term comes from Albert O. Hirschman (1970). See [[Exit]].

== F ==
; First Action
: A new Circle's first visible win on an issue its members care about, ideally a micro-action that can be done within a week. See [[Winnable issue]].

== I ==
; Imperative commitment
: A commitment that holds because breaking it is constrained or impossible. Compare motivational commitment. See [[PriFi]].
; Issue buckets
: The eight areas the Circles handbook uses to sort issues: Economy, Housing, Healthcare, Welfare, Security, Infrastructure, Institutions and Education. See [[Winnable issue]].
; Issue-cutting
: Narrowing a broad problem into a target that can realistically be won. See [[Winnable issue]].

== L ==
; λPrize (Lambda Prize)
: In the words of logos.co, "a competitive prize framework for developers shipping privacy-preserving software on the Logos stack". See [[λPrize]].
; LAN
: The Logos movement zine. Issue 1 came out in September 2026. See [[LAN]] and [[Issue 1]].
; Logos
: "The private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies", and a movement building a parallel society. See [[Logos]].
; Logos Messaging
: The Logos stack's anonymous communication layer. See [[PriFi]].
; Logos Storage
: Content-addressed storage with verifiable integrity, part of the Logos stack. See [[PriFi]].

== M ==
; Magnitizdat
: Sound recordings passed around on audio tape in the Soviet bloc. See [[Samizdat]].
; Mainnet
: The stage that follows the testnet versions on the Logos roadmap. See [[Testnet]].
; Motivational commitment
: A commitment that holds because the party could break it but prefers to keep it, for reasons such as reputation or collateral. See [[PriFi]].

== N ==
; Network state
: The Logos manifesto's aim: "a self-sovereign network state" founded on liberty, security, privacy, openness and decentralisation. See [[Logos]].
; Node
: A participant that runs the Logos blockchain. Basecamp lets users run a full node, and before mainnet users can run a node on the Logos testnet. See [[Run a node]].

== P ==
; Parallel polis
: Václav Benda's idea of building independent institutions alongside the official ones, from his 1978 essay. See [[Parallel polis]].
; Parallel society
: The goal of the Logos movement. The Circles handbook calls its creation "a form of non-violent civil resistance". See [[Parallel polis]].
; Parallel Society Playbook
: A collection of winnable issues Circles have solved, written up so other Circles can adapt them. See [[Winnable issue]].
; PriFi
: Private finance. The Logos design philosophy for financial tools on privacy-preserving, peer-to-peer infrastructure, on hardware you control. See [[PriFi]].

== R ==
; RFP
: Logos RFPs are "Funded calls for builders to ship Logos-powered applications and infrastructure." See [[RFPs]].

== S ==
; Samizdat
: Self-publishing of censored texts in the Soviet bloc, copied by hand or on typewriters. See [[Samizdat]].
; Sarafu
: A digital complementary currency in Kenya, worth roughly one Kenyan shilling. Grassroots Economics documents it as part of commitment pooling. See [[Sarafu Network]].
; Second culture
: Benda's name for independent culture outside official channels, which he called the most developed parallel structure. See [[Parallel polis]].
; Steward
: A Logos Circle organiser. Stewards organise each meeting, guide the conversation and help the group uncover a winnable issue. See [[Circles]].

== T ==
; Tamizdat
: Literature published abroad, often from smuggled manuscripts. See [[Samizdat]].
; Testnet
: The test version of the Logos network that runs before mainnet. Testnet v0.3 was released on 30 September 2026. See [[Testnet]].
; Transaction supply chain
: The seven links of a deal: discovery, diligence, negotiation, contracting, ordering, settlement and enforcement. See [[PriFi]].

== V ==
; Voice
: Complaining and pushing for change from inside a failing organisation, in Hirschman's terms. See [[Exit]].
; Voucher
: "A promise denominated in an agreed upon Unit of Account", in the Grassroots Economics glossary. See [[Commitment pooling]].

== W ==
; Winnable issue
: A clear, concrete local problem that a Logos Circle can act on and solve. See [[Winnable issue]].

== Z ==
; Zine
: A "noncommercial often homemade or online publication", usually made by one person or a small group. See [[Samizdat]].
; Zones
: The part of the Logos Blockchain that allows selective disclosure for compliance and disputes. See [[PriFi]].

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669274000,"t":"edit","title":"Harry Halpin","text":"'''Harry Halpin''' is a researcher whose work spans philosophy, artificial intelligence and privacy. He is co-founder and CEO of Nym Technologies, a privacy company. He wrote "The Anti-Palantir Manifesto", which appears in LAN [[Issue 1]] as [[Issue 1/Anti-Palantir Manifesto]].

== Background ==
Halpin completed his PhD at the University of Edinburgh under Andy Clark. He did postdoctoral work with Bernard Stiegler. He is an affiliated researcher at the Center Leo Apostel for Interdisciplinary Studies (CLEA) at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel. His more than 50 publications cover philosophy, artificial intelligence, big data, privacy, security and blockchain technology.

== The Anti-Palantir Manifesto ==
On 18 April 2026 the data company Palantir posted a 22-point manifesto on X. Halpin answered with 22 counterpoints of his own. Nym published them on its blog on 23 April 2026 as "The Anti-Palantir Manifesto". Halpin says the text sets out his personal beliefs and not those of Nym.

His main points:
* Programmers who build the internet have a moral duty to the whole world.
* Surveillance justified by foreign threats ends up aimed at immigrants, dissidents and ordinary citizens.
* Laws and moral appeals alone cannot protect privacy. In his words, surveillance "can only be defeated by building software and hardware".
* Anonymity is a precondition of freedom. He opposes biometric digital ID and favours decentralised tools and voluntary communities.
* Technologists face a choice between building tools for control and building spaces for freedom.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669320000,"t":"edit","title":"Logos","text":"'''Logos''' is a social movement and a decentralised technology stack. The stack is private by default and is built for parallel societies: communities, institutions and economies that run outside legacy systems. The movement organises people in local groups called [[Circles]].

== Mission ==
The Logos home page argues that civil society is in decline and that institutions are failing. It says reform from within will not fix this. It points to debt, the gap in wealth and home ownership between generations, surveillance, corruption and stagnant institutions.

The founding text is the manifesto ''Logos: A Declaration of Independence in Cyberspace'', by Jarrad Hope. It proposes a decentralised, privacy-preserving and politically neutral stack to support self-sovereign virtual territories and parallel societies. It calls for voluntary, consensus-based governance and for users to own the services, data and assets they rely on. The manifesto states: "Privacy is not secrecy, it is a fundamental right."

The home page lists four uses for the stack:
* secure communications
* private, censorship-resistant money
* permanent decentralised archives
* anonymous donations and mutual aid

== The stack ==
The official λPrize and RFP repositories describe three core layers:
* '''Blockchain.''' A privacy-preserving Layer 1 for execution, settlement and coordination. The '''Logos Execution Zone (LEZ)''' is where decentralised applications run. It separates public and private state, with shielded balances.
* '''Storage.''' Durable, censorship-resistant data availability for decentralised apps and file sharing.
* '''Messaging.''' Private peer-to-peer communication that resists surveillance and censorship.

The three layers are reached through '''Logos Core''', a plugin-based runtime. The home page adds a fourth area, '''Networking''', which covers node discovery, peering and a mixnet.

The Logos documentation compares the stack to an operating system. It has four layers:
# '''The runtime.''' A small core written in C++ (liblogos). It loads and unloads modules, manages their life cycle and lets modules call one another.
# '''The networking layer.''' Peer discovery, connections and a mixnet that hides who is talking to whom.
# '''Modules.''' Pluggable parts such as blockchain, storage and messaging. Anyone can write a user module.
# '''Apps.''' Applications built from modules.

[[Basecamp]] is the default desktop launcher for the stack. The '''Logos Node''' runs the same runtime without a user interface, for node operators. The documentation says privacy is built into the infrastructure, so an app inherits metadata protection whether or not its developer adds it.

The stack is in public testing. See [[Testnet]] for the release history.

== The movement ==
The movement page describes Logos as building a parallel society. It aims to help people find supportive communities, learn self-reliance skills and keep control of their money and speech, starting where they live. Its stated approach is "Action, not permission". The same page says "Technology alone won't save us."

On 9 October 2026 the movement page counted more than 2,000 activists and organisations. The home page showed 151 contributors, 226 node operators, 47 Circles and 19 winnable local issues.

The home page offers three paths:
* '''Build''' privacy-first, decentralised apps. See [[λPrize]] and [[RFPs]].
* '''Operate''' a node to secure the network. See [[Run a node]].
* '''Organise''' locally. See [[Circles]].

== Circles ==
Logos Circles are self-organised local groups. They work on [[Winnable issue|winnable issues]] such as clean-ups, issue advocacy and community fundraising. The Circles handbook says Circles meet in person at least once a month.

The handbook names three roles:
* '''Activist or participant.''' Cares about a local issue and wants to help without leading.
* '''Circle Steward.''' Brings people together and builds a local community over time.
* '''Activist Builder.''' Makes tools, systems, research, media or infrastructure. See [[Activist Builder]].

You do not need a particular background to join. See [[Getting started]] for how to join or start a Circle.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669466000,"t":"edit","title":"Medusa","text":"{{Infobox tool | name = Medusa | what = A self-custody privacy wallet for the Logos Execution Zone, run as a Basecamp module | stage = Prototype | licence = GPL-3.0 | code = https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa | use = https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa#install-a-release-no-build-tools | build = https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa#quickstart-build-from-source | verified_on = 9 October 2026 | verified_against = README, CHANGELOG and release v0.4.4 (26 August 2026) }} '''Medusa''' is a private, self-custodial wallet for the Logos Execution Zone (LEZ), built by the developer ParadoxComputer as a [[Basecamp]] module. == What it does == * Medusa holds your keys and sends public transfers, private transfers and tokens. Your keys never leave the wallet. * Private transfers come in three kinds: shield (public to private), deshield (private to public) and private to private. LAN Issue 1 notes that in private accounts the amount and the sender stay hidden. * A private transfer builds a zero-knowledge proof on your own machine. This is fast on the local devnet. On a real-proof zone it takes minutes, and the README reports 20 to 40 minutes or more on a busy machine. * Your password encrypts the keys on disk. The wallet locks itself when idle. * It ships with four zones: a local devnet, the Paradox Computer sequencer over clearnet, the same sequencer over Tor, and the Logos public testnet. You can add your own sequencer, by URL or .onion address. * '''Connect with Medusa''' is a small JavaScript SDK (@paradoxcomputer/medusa-connect). It lets another Basecamp module ask the wallet for a payment. The user approves every connection and every transfer inside the wallet. The repository includes a demo Tip Jar module. * LAN Issue 1 says it supports multiple identities in one wallet. It is part of the same developer's wider Logos work, which includes LEZ ZoneScan, an explorer for the Logos Execution Zone. Stage: Prototype. The README status line reads "v0.4.0 (testnet, LEZ v0.2.2)" and its security section says to read it "before trusting it with anything but testnet play-money." == Use it == # Download the release assets for your platform from the [https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa/releases releases page]: medusa_core and medusa_ui. Always install them as a pair. # Install them from Basecamp (Apps, then install a package), or unpack the medusa-wallet bundle and run its install.sh. The bundle needs no Nix, Rust or Tor. # Close and reopen Basecamp. It has no hot reload. # Open Medusa, choose Create wallet and set a password. Write down the 24-word recovery phrase. # On devnet, make a new account and claim the faucet (150 LEZ). Then try Send, Shield, Deshield or Private. On a Mac: the build is for Apple Silicon only and is not notarised. Clear the quarantine flag on the downloaded files first, and install tor with Homebrew for the Tor zone. Intel Macs are not built. Read the README's "Security posture" section before you use it. Three points from it: * Basecamp does not yet isolate modules from each other, so your password is the main defence. * Check the address shown next to the zone name before you send anything large. That is how you spot a wallet someone has repointed. * Each .lgx carries a signature, but Basecamp does not yet enforce a signature policy on install and the GitHub release assets are unsigned. Verify what you install. A known limit on testnet: a private account can receive only once, so the wallet offers fresh private accounts as destinations. == Build it == You need Nix with flakes, Rust (cargo), Logos Basecamp and tor. # bash wallet/build.sh clones the upstream zone at a pinned commit, applies the Medusa patches and builds the wallet and sequencers. # bash module/scripts/install-dev.sh --launch builds the module with Nix, installs it into Basecamp and restarts Basecamp. == Releases == * v0.2.3, 13 July 2026: first public release. * v0.3.0, 30 July 2026. * v0.4.0, 11 August 2026: moves to LEZ v0.2.2, adds an on-chain token faucet and closes a gap that let a locked wallet be repointed to another sequencer. * v0.4.4, 26 August 2026: the latest release. The wallet's opening screen shows the build you are running. == User reviews == Add your review on the [[Talk:Medusa|talk page]]. == See also == * [[Issue 1/Monthly Highlights]], where LAN Issue 1 lists Medusa under 11 August * [[Basecamp]] * [[Testnet]] * [[PriFi]] * [[Tools]] == Sources == * [https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa Medusa README], GitHub, updated 26 August 2026 * [https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md Medusa CHANGELOG], GitHub, entry for 0.4.0 dated 11 August 2026 * [https://github.com/ParadoxComputer/medusa/releases Medusa releases], GitHub, v0.2.3 to v0.4.4 * [https://github.com/ParadoxComputer ParadoxComputer], GitHub profile * LAN Issue 1, "Monthly Highlights", page 8, September 2026 (see [[Issue 1/Monthly Highlights]]) {{Page status|Usable}}","summary":"Parallel Wiki build: page from sourced research, source-checked 9 October 2026","as":"Eleutherious"}

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669529000,"t":"edit","title":"Parallel polis","text":"'''Parallel polis''' is the idea, set out by the Czech dissident [[Václav Benda]], that people living under an oppressive regime can build their own institutions alongside the official ones.

== The basics ==
Benda wrote the essay "The Parallel Polis" (''Paralelní polis'') for the spokespersons and signatories of [[Charter 77]]. The English translation on The Anarchist Library dates it 17 May 1978. Wikipedia's article on Benda gives 1977 as the year he wrote it.

Charter 77 was an informal civic initiative in Czechoslovakia. Its declaration was published on 6 January 1977 with 242 first signatories. It criticised the government for failing to implement its human rights commitments.

Benda proposed building parallel structures instead of only opposing the system or trying to reform it from within. The translation's foreword describes a "parallel polis" that would "exist alongside the official order". Benda wanted Charter 77 to move from a moral stance to a concrete, positive programme. He proposed parallel structures to supply missing functions, and using existing structures where possible to "humanize" them.

The essay works through areas where such structures could grow:
* a second culture, which Benda called "the most developed and most dynamic parallel structure"
* parallel education, which he called "a task of eminent importance"
* a parallel information system
* a parallel economy, founded on "a system of mutual guarantee"
* parallel political structures, including a parallel foreign policy

Benda was a mathematician with a doctorate in theoretical cybernetics (1975). After his academic career ended he worked as a computer programmer. He was arrested in May 1979, charged with subverting the state, and imprisoned until 1983.

The essay first circulated in samizdat in 1978. Benda returned to the idea in ''Social Research'' (1988). Paul Wilson's English translation appeared in ''Civic Freedom in Central Europe'' (1991) and again in ''The Long Night of the Watchman: Essays by Václav Benda, 1977-1989'' (2018). Mark Qvist made a public domain translation.

== How it applies to Logos ==
The Circles handbook's Parallel Society Playbook says "The creation of a parallel society is a form of non-violent civil resistance". It says the concept comes from Czechoslovakian dissidents living under a totalitarian regime, who called it the parallel polis. The playbook collects winnable issues that Circles have solved, so other Circles can adapt them. In its words, "Together, the issues we solve form the basis of a global parallel society."

The Logos website calls Logos "the private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies" and says "Logos is a movement building a parallel society." The Circles roadmap aims to position Logos as a "credible parallel institution".

The Circles issue buckets page names seven pillars of a parallel society: Economy, Security, Healthcare, Housing, Welfare, Infrastructure and Institutions.

== Examples ==
* Charter 77's information network. Benda wrote that "Charter 77 managed to create a parallel information system that was functional and prompt."
* Benda's own essay, which circulated as samizdat in 1978. See [[Samizdat]].
* Paralelní Polis in Prague. In 2014 a space inspired by the idea opened in Prague's Holešovice district. Wikipedia says its venues operate as cafés that accept only cryptocurrency. People inspired by it started a similar space in Bratislava.
* A Logos Circle example. The Circles handbook lists the [[Circles/Lisbon|Lisbon Circle]]'s completed campaign for a community centre for young adults.

'''Precious Plastic''' is an open community that gives away the designs for small plastic-recycling machines, so anyone who can weld can build one and run a local workshop.

== What it does ==
Recycling plastic normally needs an industrial plant. Precious Plastic shrank the machinery to fit a workshop and published the plans. There are four machines:
* a shredder that grinds bottles, caps and scrap into flakes
* an extruder that melts flakes into a continuous stream, for beams and filament
* an injection moulder that shoots melted flakes into a mould, for small objects
* a sheet press that flattens flakes in an oven into sheets you can cut like plywood

The drawings, part lists, code and video tutorials are free online. The machines use steel and parts you can buy in most countries. People run them as small businesses: they collect local waste and sell what they make from it.

LAN Issue 1 reports about 2,000 registered workshops. The latest figures cover 2024 and come from the 184 workshops that reported, about a tenth of the network. They count 1,400 tonnes recycled in 56 countries by 3,935 people.

The site says "All Precious Plastic content is shared under Creative Commons Attribution."

== Who runs it ==
* Dave Hakkens started it in 2012 as a student project at the Design Academy Eindhoven. Version 1 went online in 2013.
* Later versions followed in early 2016, late 2017 and January 2020. The site lists Version 5 as fundraising in 2025.
* The Precious Plastic Foundation, a non-profit in the Netherlands set up in 2023, runs it today. The site calls it a project of One Army.
* Memberships and donations pay for it. The three membership tiers start at €7, €12 and €60 a month, and members get a vote on priorities.

== Join or copy it ==
* Learn the machines in the [https://community.preciousplastic.com/academy/intro.html Academy].
* Find recyclers near you on the [https://community.preciousplastic.com/map community map].
* Start a workspace with the starter kits linked from the [https://www.preciousplastic.com home page].
* Join the community and ask questions at [https://community.preciousplastic.com community.preciousplastic.com].

== In LAN ==

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669532000,"t":"edit","title":"PriFi","text":"'''PriFi''', short for private finance, is the Logos design philosophy for financial tools built on privacy-preserving, peer-to-peer infrastructure, on hardware you control.

== The basics ==
The Logos PriFi thesis page calls PriFi "a technical design philosophy". It describes "financial primitives deployed on privacy-preserving, peer-to-peer infrastructure, on hardware you control."

PriFi starts from the idea of a '''transaction supply chain'''. A deal passes through seven links:
# Discovery: finding a counterparty
# Diligence: verifying who they are
# Negotiation: agreeing price and terms
# Contracting: committing in an enforceable form
# Ordering: putting transactions in sequence
# Settlement: the only link where value moves
# Enforcement and recourse: making outcomes stick, or proving what happened

The Logos blog argues that a blockchain gives strong guarantees at settlement and leaves the other links exposed. A transaction is only as secure as its least-protected link. "PriFi aims to secure the entire transaction supply chain." A later blog post by Nasrudin calls it "an approach to taking privacy across the whole lifecycle of a transaction".

The blog sorts the threats into two classes. '''Counterparty hazards''' come from the parties actually transacting. '''Predatory hazards''' come from "actors who are not party to the transaction at all", such as a competing bidder.

The blog also separates two kinds of credible commitment. A '''motivational''' commitment holds because the party could break it but prefers to keep it, for reasons such as reputation or collateral. An '''imperative''' commitment holds because breaking it is constrained or impossible. PriFi tries to shrink what the blog calls the "commitment surface".

The blog states that "PriFi, or private finance, is not about absolute secrecy, and it's not about evading regulations."

== How it applies to Logos ==
PriFi is a Logos term. The PriFi thesis page maps parts of the Logos stack to the links they protect:
* [[Basecamp]], a local desktop app: discovery and diligence
* Logos Messaging, anonymous communication: discovery, diligence and negotiation
* Logos Storage, content-addressed storage with verifiable integrity: contracting
* Logos Blockchain, Blend (private transaction and block propagation): ordering
* Logos Blockchain, Cryptarchia (private proof-of-stake consensus): settlement
* Logos Blockchain, Zones (selective disclosure for compliance and disputes): enforcement

The page names a companion paper, "Vaults of glass: why transparent blockchains are incomplete institutions". The blog post of 15 September 2026 says its research was compiled by Logos cofounder Jarrad Hope. It ties PriFi to Logos's civil society aims: "Effective parallel organising requires economic rails".

The blog post of 21 September 2026 says [[Testnet]] v0.3 advances the stack's coordination components, including Service Discovery, Mix, RLN and Chat.

== Examples ==
These are the cases Logos sources use to explain what PriFi addresses.
* The Bybit theft (2025, $1.5 billion). The attack compromised the signing interface. The chain then executed the signed instruction.
* Address poisoning, maximal extractable value (MEV) and frontrunning, which the blog lists as threats.
* A UK merger and acquisition leak that, per the PriFi thesis page, added £42M to the cost of an acquisition.
* Physical coercion attacks in crypto, which the thesis page puts at over $100M in losses from January to April 2026.
* Bitcoin nodes, which reject any transaction that breaks the protocol's rules. The blog gives this as an imperative commitment.
* Muster, where a 2-of-3 authorisation rule means no single participant can act alone.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669535000,"t":"edit","title":"RFPs","text":"{{Infobox project | name = Logos RFP Program | what = Grants for builders to deliver set pieces of work on the Logos stack | run_by = Logos | status = Active | licence = Funded work is open source under MIT and Apache 2.0 unless agreed otherwise | website = https://github.com/logos-co/rfp | join = Read an open RFP, then submit a proposal as a GitHub issue }} The '''Logos RFP Program''' gives grants to independent developers and teams. Each Request for Proposals (RFP) describes a tool, piece of infrastructure, application or integration that the [[Logos]] ecosystem needs. Builders answer with a proposal. Funded projects can range from prototypes to near-production applications. == Focus areas == Proposals should fit one of three categories: * Developer tooling and infrastructure * Applications and integrations * Ecosystem and community enablement Each RFP has a size tier, from XS to XL. For example, RFP-005 is tier L, with an estimated six months of work for a team already working on LEZ. == How to apply == # Browse the open RFPs in the [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp RFP repository] or on the [https://logos.co/builders-hub/rfps Builders Hub]. # Read the full RFP file in the RFPs folder. # Open a [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/issues/new?template=proposal.yml proposal issue] using the template. Pick the RFP from the list. # Use your proposal issue for questions. Logos posts updates there or through your contact details. The proposal template asks for: * project name, team name and a contact * team members, their links, roles and status (full-time, part-time or contractor) * a summary and a technical approach * milestones, payouts and a timeline * the total budget requested, in US dollars * relevant experience and a plan for after delivery * agreement to the RFP terms and to open-source licensing == How a proposal is reviewed == * '''Timing.''' Logos reviews proposals weekly and usually replies within 14 days. * '''Criteria.''' Proposals are judged against the RFP itself. Logos may also weigh technical feasibility, ecosystem impact, budget, team experience, compliance and reputational risk. * '''Dialogue.''' Logos may ask questions or suggest changes to milestones, budget or scope. * '''Selection.''' A notice that a proposal is going forward is not binding. A grant exists only once a written Grant Agreement is signed. Logos may ask for identity, compliance or financial details first. * '''Milestones.''' Work runs in milestones set in the Grant Agreement. Each milestone of an accepted proposal is tracked as its own GitHub issue so engineers can review it on its own. * '''No reasons owed.''' Logos does not have to explain a decision. An example of milestone review is the RFP-003 atomic swaps grant, awarded to Gateway.fm. Its review thread splits the work into seven milestones and records each decision. The reviewer writes that acceptance means "the code does what the milestone asks on LEZ testnet". Security is judged by a third-party audit in the last milestone. == Open RFPs == Status as given in the repository on 9 October 2026. {| class="wikitable" ! RFP !! Title !! Tier !! Status !! Deadline |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-005-multisig-and-coordination.md RFP-005] || Multisig and Coordination || L || Open || 16 October 2026 |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-012-curated-lending-vaults.md RFP-012] || Curated Lending Vaults || L || Closed, reopening soon || None set |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-014-liquidation-auction-engine.md RFP-014] || Liquidation and Auction Engine || L || Closed, reopening soon || None set |} === RFP-005: Multisig and Coordination === RFP-005 asks for an audited M-of-N multisig program on LEZ, private by default. It comes with an encrypted coordination room for each multisig, built on the Logos chat module. The deliverables include a Logos module API, a command-line tool and a [[Basecamp]] mini-app. Proposals must name at least one tier-1 audit firm and include the audit in the budget. Benchmarks must use real proving. The forum announcement was posted on 30 September 2026 and submissions close on 16 October 2026. == Closed RFPs == RFP-001 Admin Authority Library, RFP-002 Freeze Authority Library, RFP-003 Atomic Swaps with LEZ, RFP-004 Privacy-Preserving DEX, RFP-008 Lending and Borrowing Protocol, RFP-013 Reflexive Stablecoin Protocol, RFP-015 Token Launchpad: Bonding Curve, RFP-016 Token Launchpad: LBP, RFP-017 Privacy-Preserving Token Vesting, RFP-019 On-Chain TWAP Oracle and RFP-020 RedStone Off-Chain Oracle Adaptor for LEZ. == RFP or λPrize? == An RFP grant is agreed before work starts and is paid against milestones. A [[λPrize]] is claimed after the work is built and in use. == See also == * [[λPrize]] * [[Still to build]] * [[Getting started]] * [[FAQ]] == Sources == * [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp Logos RFP Program README], github.com/logos-co, last updated 6 October 2026 * [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/TERMS_AND_CONDITIONS.md Logos RFP Program Terms and Conditions], github.com/logos-co * [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/tree/master/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE RFP proposal and milestone templates], github.com/logos-co * [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-005-multisig-and-coordination.md RFP-005: Multisig and Coordination], github.com/logos-co * [https://forum.logos.co/t/new-rfp-rfp-005-multisig-and-coordination/1973 New RFP: RFP-005 Multisig and Coordination], Logos Forum, 30 September 2026 * [https://forum.logos.co/t/rfp-003-atomic-swaps-with-lez-gateway-fms-build-and-where-the-review-stands/1996 RFP-003 Atomic Swaps with LEZ: Gateway.fm's build and where the review stands], Logos Forum, 9 October 2026 * [https://logos.co/builders-hub/rfps RFPs], Logos Builders Hub, read 9 October 2026 {{Page status|Usable}} [[Category:Logos]]","summary":"Parallel Wiki build: page from sourced research, source-checked 9 October 2026","as":"Eleutherious"}

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669536000,"t":"edit","title":"Run a node","text":"This page summarises how to run a [[Logos]] node on the public [[Testnet]]. It follows the official guide. Use the official docs for the exact commands, because versions and bootstrap peers change between releases. == Which version this covers == The official guide at [https://docs.logos.co/run-a-node docs.logos.co/run-a-node] says it is accurate for '''Testnet v0.3'''. It pins these packages: * logosctl 0.3.2 (the command-line tool that starts and controls the node) * blockchain_module 0.3.1 * storage_module 3.0.2 * delivery_module 0.3.2 The docs note that package versions are pinned on their own and need not match the testnet number. Check the version box at the top of each docs page before you start. == Choose a route == * '''Full node from the command line.''' Runs blockchain, storage and delivery together on a Linux server. Guide: [https://docs.logos.co/run-a-node Run a Logos node with blockchain, storage, and delivery]. * '''Blockchain node only, from the command line.''' Guide: [https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-a-logos-blockchain-node-from-cli Run a Logos Blockchain node on the public testnet from the CLI]. This page says it is accurate for Testnet v0.3.0 and installs blockchain_module 0.3.0. It supports Linux x86_64, recent macOS on Apple silicon, and Raspberry Pi 5. * '''Blockchain node from Basecamp.''' Guide: [https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-a-logos-blockchain-node-from-basecamp Run a Logos Blockchain node from Basecamp]. On 9 October 2026 the node programme page said this guide still covers Testnet v0.2.1. See [[Basecamp]]. == What you need == For the full node, the official guide asks for: * a Linux host with a public IPv4 address * root or sudo access * ports 3000/udp, 8090/udp, 8091/tcp, 9000/udp, 30303/tcp and 30303/udp open on the firewall, and forwarded if you are behind NAT * a CPU with 2 cores at 2 GHz. On x86_64 it must support the ADX instruction. Generic virtual machine CPU models such as kvm64 and qemu64 hide ADX and make the blockchain module crash. * 1 GB of RAM * 1 to 2 GB free on an SSD for testnet use * a reliable connection with about 1 Mbps of free bandwidth To take part in the Blend Network you also need a stable external IP address and a low-latency connection. The docs recommend 10 Mbps or more. == Steps == These steps follow the full-node guide. The guide has the commands. # '''Install logosctl.''' Download the logosctl 0.3.2 release archive. Check its SHA-256 digest, extract it and install it as /usr/local/bin/logosctl. # '''Prepare the host.''' Create a logos system user and the data directory /var/lib/logos-node. Open the ports listed above. # '''Install the modules.''' As the logos user, start the daemon, refresh the module catalogue and install the three pinned modules by their root hashes. Installing a module does not load it. # '''Start the node.''' Run logosctl daemon start in one terminal. Use a second terminal for module commands. # '''Start the blockchain module.''' The 0.3.1 blockchain module starts a new chain with a new genesis, so the state directory must be empty. Balances and Blend declarations from the old chain do not carry over. Write the bootstrap peer file, load the module and generate user_config.yaml and keystore.yaml. Restrict both files to your user and never publish user_config.yaml. # '''Fund the node by mining.''' Once the node reports Online, start proof-of-work mining. Rewards are claimed to your node's key automatically. Mining is off by default and stops on restart, so start it again after each restart. # '''Join the Blend Network (optional).''' Fund the Blend keys from your keystore by mining, then follow the Blend guide linked from the docs. # '''Check storage.''' With logosctl 0.3.2 the storage module starts automatically. Check that it is running before you download anything. # '''Start delivery.''' Configure and start the delivery module. Delivery enables QUIC by default, so port 30303 must be open for both TCP and UDP. # '''Check the node is healthy.''' Query the daemon, list the loaded modules, check the bound ports and check the blockchain sync state. # '''Run unattended (optional).''' The guide gives a systemd service for the node and a separate start-up script for the modules. The docs warn against calling pow_status or pow_claimable_rewards before the node is Online. While the node is bootstrapping these calls never return, and later blockchain commands fail until you restart the daemon. == Bootstrap nodes for the 0.3.0 genesis == On 9 October 2026 a forum thread asked operators to join the Logos 0.3.0 genesis as bootstrap nodes. It has three steps: # With the module installed and the daemon running, load blockchain_module and call generate_user_config. This writes user_config.yaml and keystore.yaml. # Find the stake public key in keystore.yaml and post it as a reply in the thread. # Back up keystore.yaml. The genesis stake is assigned to that key and the module will not generate a second keystore in the same place. The post warns: "Lose the file, lose the stake." Read the [https://forum.logos.co/t/join-the-logos-0-3-0-genesis-as-a-bootstrap-node/1992 thread] before you post. == Earlier versions == The roadmap keeps a [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/logos-node-operator-guide Testnet v0.2.1 node operator guide], dated 7 September 2026. It pins older packages and is kept for reference. Use the docs for the current release. == See also == * [[Testnet]] * [[Basecamp]] * [[Getting started]] * [[FAQ]] * [[Logos]] == Sources == * [https://docs.logos.co/run-a-node Run a Logos node with blockchain, storage, and delivery], Logos documentation, Testnet v0.3 * [https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/get-started/run-a-logos-blockchain-node-from-cli Run a Logos Blockchain node on the public testnet from the CLI], Logos documentation, Testnet v0.3.0 * [https://forum.logos.co/t/join-the-logos-0-3-0-genesis-as-a-bootstrap-node/1992 Join the Logos 0.3.0 genesis as a bootstrap node], Logos Forum, 9 October 2026 * [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v03-release Testnet version 0.3: release notes], Logos roadmap * [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/logos-node-operator-guide Testnet version 0.2.1: Node Operator Guide], Logos roadmap, 7 September 2026 * [https://logos.co/node-programme Node Programme], logos.co, read 9 October 2026 {{Page status|Usable}} [[Category:Logos]]","summary":"Parallel Wiki build: page from sourced research, source-checked 9 October 2026","as":"Eleutherious"}

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669537000,"t":"edit","title":"Samizdat","text":"'''Samizdat''' is the self-publishing of censored texts in the Soviet bloc, copied by hand or on typewriters and passed from reader to reader.

== The basics ==
The word joins the Russian ''sam'' ("self") and ''izdat'', short for ''izdatel'stvo'' ("publishing house"). Wikipedia describes samizdat as "a form of dissident activity across the Eastern Bloc".

Texts were copied by hand or typed. A typist could make several copies at once with carbon or tissue paper, which were cheap and easy to hide. People preferred private typewriters because using an official photocopier needed authorisation.

Related forms:
* '''Tamizdat''': work published abroad, often from manuscripts smuggled out.
* '''Magnitizdat''': sound recordings passed around on audio tape.

Eugeniusz Smolar, a Polish dissident who left Poland in 1970, writes that "Samizdat was known since the late 1940s in Poland". It stayed rare there until 1976, when the Workers' Defence Committee (KOR) helped start a large underground press. Smolar describes a cycle he calls the "Circle of Hope". Samizdat circulated at home. Tamizdat came in from exile. Western radio stations such as Radio Free Europe, the BBC and Voice of America read banned texts on air. In his words, "Every broadcast was repeated several times over the course of a week."

Zines are a related form. A zine is a "noncommercial often homemade or online publication", usually made by one person or a small group. Wikipedia notes that Ukrainian samizdat (''samvydav'') continues today, with zines and artbooks as its most common forms. In hacker jargon, "samizdat" means sharing needed documents that are hard to get.

== How it applies to Logos ==
LAN is the Logos movement zine. Its first issue, from September 2026, has an article on samizdat. See [[Issue 1/Samizdat]].

== Examples ==
* ''A Chronicle of Current Events'', the longest-running samizdat periodical. It ran from 1968 to 1982, across 65 issues, and was dedicated to defending human rights.
* Poland's ''drugi obieg'' ("second circuit") of publishing, which grew from the mid-1970s. Smolar describes underground titles such as ''Zapis'' and ''Tygodnik Mazowsze''.
* ''Aneks'', a political quarterly made by Smolar's group in exile in Sweden.
* [[Václav Benda]]'s essay [[The Parallel Polis]], which first circulated in samizdat in 1978.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669538000,"t":"edit","title":"Sarafu Network","text":"{{Infobox project
