| status   = Active
| website  = https://sarafu.network
| join     = Create a voucher or join a commitment pool through the Cosmo-Local Credit App at cosmolocal.credit
}}
'''Sarafu Network''' is a platform from Grassroots Economics in Kenya where communities issue vouchers for their goods and services and put them into shared pools to swap with each other.

== What it does ==
* A member creates a voucher that stands for a future commitment, for example a gift card for a product or service.
* Vouchers go into shared pools, so communities can swap goods and services through them.
* Grassroots Economics calls this [[Commitment pooling|commitment pooling]]: "A protocol and practice for routing promises, settlement, and mutual support through shared pools." The vouchers are called Community Asset Vouchers.
* The Grassroots Economics site reports 188 active commitment pools and 745 active vouchers on the Celo blockchain.

=== Move to Cosmo-Local Credit ===
The Grassroots Economics documentation says the service "formerly presented as Sarafu Network transitioned to Cosmo-Local Credit." The current app is at [https://cosmolocal.credit cosmolocal.credit]. The documentation warns that not every old Sarafu account, voucher, pool or balance moved across or is still available. The Grassroots Economics "Get involved" page still points communities to sarafu.network to start a pool.

== Who runs it ==
* Grassroots Economics is a non-profit registered in Kenya. It says it has supported community economies since 2010. It is based in Kilifi.
* The CLC history page says the Grassroots Economics Foundation built and ran the old Sarafu Network and now operates the CLC App.
* The Foundation does not issue the vouchers people create, and it does not run their pools. Each issuer and each Pool Steward answers for their own commitments and rules.

== Join or copy it ==
* Read the [https://docs.cosmolocal.credit/introduction/getting-started CLC getting-started guide]. You must be 18 or over. Before you use a pool, check its steward, admitted vouchers, fees and credit limit.
* Grassroots Economics offers new Pool Stewards a free consultation, training for organisers, platform access at no cost and ongoing support. See [https://grassrootseconomics.org/get-involved Get involved].
* Field guides for creating vouchers and running operations are at [https://docs.grassecon.org/ops/ docs.grassecon.org].
* To copy or build on it: the site says "All our code is open-source." The code is on GitHub at [https://github.com/grassrootseconomics grassrootseconomics] and [https://github.com/cosmolocalcredit cosmolocalcredit]. Check the licence in each repository.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669539000,"t":"edit","title":"Still to build","text":"This follows the Free Software Directory's [https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/Collection:High_Priority_Projects "High Priority Projects"] list.

This page lists things the [[Logos]] movement needs built that nobody has built yet. Each item is an open [[λPrize]] or an open [[RFPs|RFP]]. Status is as given in the official repositories on 9 October 2026. Check the linked file before you start, because prizes close when someone wins them.

== Open λPrizes ==
You build first, get real users, then claim. See [[λPrize]] for the rules.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0021.md LP-0021: LEZ Wallet and Provider SDK]''' ($20,000, X-Large). A wallet for one Logos Execution Zone with public and private accounts, plus an SDK that lets other apps ask the wallet for approval.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0026.md LP-0026: Forum App]''' ($5,500, Large). A public forum that protects its users' privacy. Judges look for meaningful use, for example by Logos [[Circles]].
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0001.md LP-0001: NFT Wallet Support and Private Ownership Proof]''' ($5,000, Medium). NFT support for a LEZ wallet, with a way to prove you hold an NFT from a collection without showing which one.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0023.md LP-0023: LEZ Program Registry]''' ($2,000, Medium). A registry where developers publish deployed programs with names, interfaces and source links, and anyone can check the code matches.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0018.md LP-0018: OpenStreetMap integration]''' ($1,500, Medium). A [[Basecamp]] app and SDK to host and download OpenStreetMap data through Logos Storage, with checksums.

== Draft λPrizes ==
These are written but not yet open.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0022.md LP-0022: Combined Blockchain and Zone Wallet]''' ($10,000, Large). Extends the LP-0021 wallet to the base chain, staking, bridging and many zones.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0004.md LP-0004: Sealed-Bid Auction Using Shielded Balances]''' (amount to be decided). An on-chain auction where bids stay hidden. Waiting for a LEZ timelock feature.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0011.md LP-0011: Minimal Rust SDK for LEZ programs]''' (amount to be decided). A light SDK that removes repeated plumbing from LEZ programs. Under review for overlap with the LEZ framework.

== Open RFPs ==
You apply with a proposal first, then build under a grant. See [[RFPs]] for the process.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-005-multisig-and-coordination.md RFP-005: Multisig and Coordination]''' (tier L). An audited M-of-N multisig on LEZ, private by default, with an encrypted room for signers. Proposals close on 16 October 2026. [https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/issues/new?template=proposal.yml Submit a proposal].

== RFPs reopening soon ==
The RFP repository marks these as closed and "Reopening soon".
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-012-curated-lending-vaults.md RFP-012: Curated Lending Vaults]''' (tier L). A vault layer that spreads deposits across isolated lending markets, built on the RFP-008 lending protocol.
* '''[https://github.com/logos-co/rfp/blob/master/RFPs/RFP-014-liquidation-auction-engine.md RFP-014: Liquidation and Auction Engine]''' (tier L). A liquidation and auction system for collateralised debt protocols on LEZ.

== More ideas ==
The [https://github.com/logos-co/ideas Logos Community Idea Board] collects project ideas from the community.

The Logos Blog announced it on 30 September 2026. On 9 October 2026 the Logos Forum asked node operators to join the Logos 0.3.0 genesis as bootstrap nodes. See [[Run a node]]. == Release history == {| class="wikitable" ! Version !! Date !! Main changes !! Notes |- | v0.1 || No release date given on the roadmap || First test of the backends: blockchain with LEZ, storage and messaging. Alpha modules and simple apps. LEZ ran on a single central sequencer. || [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v01 Scope] |- | v0.2 || 30 June 2026 || Blend Network for block proposers. Bridging between the base layer and LEZ. Group chat without a central server. App Manager and package manager in Basecamp. || [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v02-release Release notes] |- | v0.2.1 || 2 August 2026 (release notes), 5 August 2026 (forum) || Transaction fees on the base layer. Faster first sync. Bridged funds can take part in staking. NAT traversal for storage. || [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v02-1-release Release notes], [https://forum.logos.co/t/1856 forum] |- | v0.3 || 30 September 2026 (blog) || Proof-of-work onboarding. Decentralised sequencing for LEZ. Downloads over the mixnet. The logosctl tool. Windows support. || [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/v03-release Release notes], [https://blog.logos.co/article/logos-testnet-v03-live blog] |} == v0.1 == The roadmap says v0.1 was mainly a test of the backends. UX and developer experience were left for v0.2. It shipped alpha modules for the LEZ wallet, blockchain, storage, chat and an early delivery module. Simple apps covered a blockchain wallet, a LEZ wallet with a faucet, one-to-one chat, file sharing and a mixnet demo. Users could stake, run validators and send tokens. Key exchange for chat was done outside the app, which the roadmap calls "bad UX". == v0.2 == The v0.2 release notes are dated 30 June 2026. Main changes: * '''LEZ.''' A LEZ module that other modules can use to prove and sign transactions. An indexer and an explorer. Bridging between the base layer and LEZ. Accounts owned by a group. Oracle, token and DEX programs deployed. * '''Blockchain.''' The Blend Network protects block proposers. Decentralised sequencing through the Zone SDK. The node can run through Basecamp. * '''Storage.''' Anonymous DHT queries over the mixnet. The storage module deployed to testnet. * '''Messaging.''' A unified delivery library. Group chats built on de-MLS with no central server. One-to-one chat rebuilt with multi-device support. * '''Basecamp.''' An App Manager, a refreshed package manager and process isolation for apps. == v0.2.1 == The v0.2.1 release notes are dated 2 August 2026. The forum announcement followed on 5 August 2026. Main changes: * Inscriptions on the base layer now carry fees. LEZ transactions stay free for now. * New nodes sync faster through a BitTorrent-style download. * Bridged funds can still take part in staking. * LEZ accounts must be initialised before use, and the wallet has a button for it. * Storage adds better NAT traversal. * Direct chats now use de-MLS, like group chats. Known issue: LEZ withdrawals were turned off until LEZ supports the new channel ledger. A [https://roadmap.logos.co/testnets/logos-node-operator-guide node operator guide] for v0.2.1 followed on 7 September 2026. == v0.3 == The Logos Blog announced v0.3 on 30 September 2026. Main changes: * '''Proof-of-work onboarding.''' A new route in: participants earn testnet tokens by doing computational work, so no one has to approve a request first. * '''LEZ.''' Decentralised sequencing, fees for public transactions, cross-zone messages, events and program upgrades. Programs now record changes as diffs, which breaks existing programs. * '''Blockchain.''' Zone sequencers can stake bridged funds on the base layer. A new Logos SQL zone turns a channel into a shared SQL database. * '''Storage.''' Downloads can travel over the mixnet. Storage also serves as the back end for the package manager. * '''Messaging.''' Spam protection with RLN, message history and offline retrieval. * '''Basecamp and Core.''' A Monero wallet and Ethereum wallet apps. The single logosctl tool replaces three older tools. Windows support. Known issues listed in the notes: * Chat accounts do not persist yet. Reopening Chat creates a new account. * RLN proof checks switch on about two weeks after release. * Faster downloads over the mixnet are planned for v0.4. The docs say the 0.3.1 blockchain module starts a new chain with a new genesis. Nodes must start with an empty state directory. == Next == The v0.3 notes and blog name '''v0.4''' as the next version. The blog says smaller breaking changes to LEZ are possible in v0.4. {"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669544000,"t":"edit","title":"The Parallel Polis","text":"'''"The Parallel Polis"''' (Czech: ''Paralelní polis'') is an essay by the Czech dissident [[Václav Benda]], dated 17 May 1978. Benda wrote it as a discussion paper for the spokespeople and signatories of [[Charter 77]]. It argues that dissidents should build parallel structures to supply what the official ones fail to provide. It gave the idea of a [[Parallel polis]] its name. A free English translation has been in the public domain since January 2026.

== Publication history ==
* '''1978, samizdat.''' Benda dated the essay 17 May 1978. It circulated in [[Samizdat]]. According to its 2026 translator, its original Czech title was "Pro mluvčí a signatáře Charty 77" (For Spokespersons and Signatories of Charter 77).
* '''1980, Cologne.''' It was printed in the émigré collection ''O svobodě a moci'' (On Freedom and Power), published by Index in Cologne.
* '''1985, sequel.''' Benda revisited the idea in "The Meaning, Context, and Legacy of the Parallel Polis".
* '''1988, ''Social Research''.''' The journal ''Social Research'' (volume 55, 1988) ran "Parallel Polis, or An Independent Society in Central and Eastern Europe: An Inquiry". It had an introduction by H. Gordon Skilling and contributions from Benda, Milan Šimečka, Ivan Martin Jirous, Jiří Dienstbier, Václav Havel, Ladislav Hejdánek and Jan Šimsa. The 2026 translator lists it as a later reflection on the essay, separate from a translation of it.
* '''1991, first full English translation.''' Paul Wilson's translation, "The Parallel 'Polis'", appeared in ''Civic Freedom in Central Europe: Voices from Czechoslovakia'' (Palgrave Macmillan, 1991), edited by H. Gordon Skilling and Paul Wilson. The essay fills pages 35 to 41. The same book carries Czech responses to it and a chapter by Martin Palouš, "Jan Patočka versus Václav Benda".
* '''2018, collected essays.''' According to the 2026 translator, Wilson's translation was reprinted in ''The Long Night of the Watchman: Essays by Václav Benda, 1977–1989'' (St. Augustine's Press, 2018), edited by F. Flagg Taylor IV.
* '''2026, public domain translation.''' In January 2026 Mark Qvist published a new English translation from the Czech and released it into the public domain. He worked mainly from a Czech text published by Scriptum, which its editor confirms is complete. His foreword says the Wilson translation is held back by copyright, paywalls and small print runs.

== What it argues ==
Benda starts from a question Charter 77 faced after its first year: what next? The Charter had stayed within the law and drawn in people of many views. But its stress on ethics over politics was running out of force. Patočka had died, the regime had switched to quiet pressure, and the movement's moral stance had no positive content. Benda saw the last point as decisive.

He sets aside two paths. Open confrontation with the regime would be suicidal. Reform and compromise could not win public trust under the conditions of the time. His third way is to build, step by step, "parallel structures" that supply what the official ones fail to provide. Where possible, the movement should also make existing structures more humane.

He sets out a programme in six areas.
* '''Law.''' The legal system is vague. Its gaps should be used by testing limits and holding any ground gained. The aim is to shift from a default where everything is banned to one where everything is allowed unless a rule says otherwise.
* '''Culture.''' The "second culture" is the most developed parallel structure and the model for the rest. Criticism, journalism, theatre and film need more support.
* '''Education and scholarship.''' Parallel education matters a great deal, for each person and for society. Benda wants an ambitious programme here.
* '''Information.''' The Charter's early samizdat network reached tens of thousands of people but had decayed. Distribution deserves as much care as writing. Networks should grow outside Prague, and copying methods should improve.
* '''Economy.''' The regime uses economic pressure to break people. The movement needs mutual material support, charity, international solidarity and independent income.
* '''Politics and foreign policy.''' The movement should prepare ground for parallel political life, from civic education to political groupings. Publicity abroad protects people from arbitrary power. Links with similar movements elsewhere in the Eastern bloc were weak and need study.

Benda expects the parallel structures to outgrow the Charter. They will need their own autonomy, or they will turn into a ghetto. The Charter should help them into being, vouch for their legality and keep documenting abuses in plain language. If the plan partly works, the official structures will come under pressure. They will either break down or be restored to useful work. The end goal is a "parallel polis": a community of citizens who live with dignity and in truth.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669545000,"t":"edit","title":"Tools","text":"Software you install and run.

The core Logos software, [[Basecamp]] and the node, has its own pages under [[Logos]]. See [[Basecamp]] and [[Run a node]].

== Tools ==
* [[Booth]]: broadcast a live stream from Basecamp over Logos Messaging, with no server or account. Prototype.
* [[Medusa]]: a self-custody privacy wallet for the Logos Execution Zone, run as a Basecamp module. Prototype.

Each tool page has a stage: Design, Planning, Prototype, Almost done or Full Release. The page says which line from the project's own sources set the stage.

== Criteria for listing a tool ==
The format of these criteria comes from [https://www.privacyguides.org/en/about/criteria/ Privacy Guides] and its [https://www.privacyguides.org/en/vpn/ VPN criteria], which split each test into a minimum and a best case. A tool must meet every minimum to be listed here. The best case is what we hope to see.

=== Open source licence ===
'''Minimum to qualify:'''
* Released under a licence approved by the Open Source Initiative or the Free Software Foundation.
* The licence is named in the repository.
'''Best case:'''
* A copyleft or permissive licence that matches the rest of the Logos stack.
* Every dependency it ships is also open source.

=== Published code ===
'''Minimum to qualify:'''
* All source code is public in a repository anyone can read.
* A reader can build it from that source.
'''Best case:'''
* Versioned releases with notes on what changed.
* Signed releases, and builds that can be reproduced.
* Dependencies pinned to exact versions.

=== Documentation ===
'''Minimum to qualify:'''
* Install and use instructions a newcomer can follow.
* Build instructions.
'''Best case:'''
* A step-by-step guide from zero to working.
* A plain statement of known limits and the threat model: what it protects against and what it does not.

=== Privacy ===
'''Minimum to qualify:'''
* No analytics, telemetry or tracking.
* No account or personal information needed to use it.
'''Best case:'''
* Works over Tor or another anonymity network.
* Keeps no logs or records of its users.
* Keys and secrets stay on the user's own device.

=== Who maintains it ===
'''Minimum to qualify:'''
* A named maintainer or team, or a public handle with a history of commits.
* Some way to report bugs, such as an issue tracker.
'''Best case:'''
* More than one active maintainer.
* A security policy, a way to disclose bugs in private and an independent audit.
* Says clearly whether it is an official Logos product or a community project.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669546000,"t":"edit","title":"Václav Benda","text":"'''Václav Benda''' (1946 to 1999) was a Czech Catholic philosopher, mathematician and dissident. He signed [[Charter 77]] and served twice as one of its spokespeople. In 1978 he wrote "[[The Parallel Polis]]", the essay that gave the idea of a [[Parallel polis]] its name. He spent four years in prison for his human rights work. After 1989 he became a politician.

== Life ==
Benda was born in Prague on 8 August 1946, the son of a lawyer. He studied philosophy at Charles University in Prague and took a doctorate in philosophy in 1970. He then studied mathematics and physics and completed a doctorate in theoretical cybernetics in 1975. His supervisor was Ivan Havel, the brother of Václav Havel. Through him Benda met opposition circles.

In 1968 he was active in the student movement and chaired the students' council of the Faculty of Philosophy. He also founded the Young Catholics Club. He was a devout Roman Catholic. This was unusual among the leaders of Charter 77. His academic career ended in the early 1970s when he refused to join the Communist Party.

He worked as a computer programmer at the Railways Research Institute. He was dismissed after signing Charter 77 and then worked as a stoker. He married the mathematician Kamila Bendová (born Neubauerová). They had six children. Their flat in Prague became a refuge for people harassed by the regime.

Benda took part in the 1976 meetings that led to Charter 77. He became one of its spokespeople on 1 February 1978. In April 1978 he co-founded the Committee for the Defence of the Unjustly Persecuted (VONS). VONS publicised the fate of people associated with the Charter.

On 29 May 1979 the secret police (StB) arrested ten VONS members. Benda was one of them. On 22 and 23 October 1979 the Prague Municipal Court tried six of them, Benda and Havel included. Benda was sentenced to four years for subversion. He was released on 29 May 1983 and went back to work for Charter 77 and VONS. He served as a Charter 77 spokesperson again from 1 January 1984 to early 1985.

In 1985 he started the underground Christian magazine ''Paraf''. In 1988 he helped draft the manifesto ''Democracy for All''.

In November 1989 he founded the Christian Democratic Party (KDS) and became its first chairman. He was elected to parliament in 1990. He chaired the Chamber of the Nations of the Federal Assembly from 25 June to 31 December 1992. The KDS later merged with the Civic Democratic Party (ODS). In the 1990s he headed the state office that investigated crimes of the Communist era. In 1996 he was elected to the Czech Senate for Prague 1. He held the seat until his death.

He met General Augusto Pinochet when Pinochet visited Prague in 1994. He defended Pinochet, with qualifications. ''City Journal'' notes that this damaged Benda's standing. He died in Prague in June 1999 after a long illness. Sources differ on the exact day (1 or 2 June).

== The parallel polis ==
Benda dated his best-known essay 17 May 1978. He wrote it as a discussion paper for Charter 77's spokespeople and signatories. It circulated in samizdat. In it he proposed that dissidents build "parallel structures" for the functions the official ones failed to serve: law, culture, education, information, the economy, and politics and foreign policy. Over time these could add up to a "parallel polis", a community of citizens living in dignity and truth. In 1985 he wrote a sequel, "The Meaning, Context, and Legacy of the Parallel Polis". See [[The Parallel Polis]] for the text, its translations and a summary.

His essays from 1977 to 1989 appeared in English in 2018 as ''The Long Night of the Watchman'', edited by F. Flagg Taylor IV.

A space in Prague named Parallel Polis was inspired by his idea. Its café accepts only cryptocurrency.

== Why it matters to Logos ==
Logos describes itself as "the private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies". Its homepage says the right response to broken systems is to "build alongside them, and eventually, beyond them".

On 12 June 2025 Logos held a Circles meetup in Brno on Benda's essay. The event page says Benda wrote it "during the dark days of communist oppression" and that "the need for parallel societies lives on". The meetup set out to discuss what can be learned from the essay and how to apply its strongest ideas now.

The LAN article [[Issue 1/Parallel Society]] in [[Issue 1]] tells his story.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669547000,"t":"edit","title":"Winnable issue","text":"A '''winnable issue''' is a clear, concrete local problem that a Logos Circle can act on and solve, chosen to bring a community together and build momentum towards bigger goals.

== The basics ==
The Circles handbook says organising "involves selecting a clear, concrete, winnable issue". The issue lets organisers mobilise a community, build solidarity and gain momentum.

The handbook places the idea within community organising, where "there is a concept known as an 'issue-cutting' or 'issue-based campaign' strategy." It quotes Saul Alinsky's ''Rules for Radicals'': "Pick the target, freeze it, personalize it, and polarize it." It also links to a Status note on Interaction Ritual Chains.

An issue is winnable when it:
* aligns with Logos values: decentralisation, privacy, open infrastructure and autonomy
* carries emotional weight for the people affected
* is tangible and achievable, so the Circle can act and see progress
* already has local roots, in people, groups or organisations working on it

The handbook's checklist asks four things. Is the issue clear enough to explain in one or two sentences? Does it move people to act? Can the Circle take concrete steps, with clear signs of success and a clear start and finish? Does it fit values such as decentralisation, transparency, privacy or mutual aid? "If you can check at least 80% of this list", it is likely a real winnable issue. If not, refine the problem or do more community listening.

The Circles Charter adds limits. "Every Circle is built around an initial, pre-defined winnable issue." It must be completable within three months, have visible local impact, be doable by volunteers and produce a measurable outcome. Its goal for the first Circle is to complete or materially deliver the winnable issue within 30 days of launch.

=== From problem to win ===
The handbook's pipeline has five steps:
# Community listening: ask what problems people see and what is missing.
# Cut the issue: "Choose a narrow, winnable target that targets part of the larger problem."
# Co-design with the local community: bring in partners and test the idea with the people affected.
# Prototype using Circle capabilities: build with the community and produce something visible, such as a working tool, a documented process or a public demonstration.
# Impact signal: track two or three simple measures, such as active participants or local adoption.

The Circles issue buckets page advises starting with one visible win, which it calls the '''First Action'''. It suggests a problem people recognise locally and a micro-action that can be done within a week. It sorts issues into eight buckets: Economy and Cost of Living, Housing, Healthcare, Welfare and Social Protection, Security and Crime, Infrastructure, Rule of Law and Institutions, and Education and Learning.

== How it applies to Logos ==
Winnable issues are the core of Logos Circles. The Logos movement page says "Logos Circles are self-organised groups solving winnable issues that matter locally" and "Local Circles are solving winnable issues every week."

Under the Circles Charter, Stewards design the Circle's first winnable issue during training and publish Circle reports. The Parallel Society Playbook asks Circles to write up the issues they solved, including why each one was winnable, so other Circles can adapt them. It says "Together, the issues we solve form the basis of a global parallel society."

== Examples ==
The pipeline page turns large problems into winnable ones:
* Dirty streets: a trash clean-up day.
* Youth unemployment: fundraising for a school's IT department.
* Food insecurity: setting up a food bank.
* Digital exclusion of older people: in-person digital literacy sessions.
* Isolation among domestic violence survivors: a safe communication channel.

Winnable issues Circles have completed, from the handbook's list:
* [[Circles/Lisbon|Lisbon]]: a community centre for young adults. The local government confirmed the space and community leaders received the keys.
* [[Circles/Zanzibar|Zanzibar]]: Raspberry Pi computers for a school. Funds were raised and devices donated, against a target of $2,000 for 10 devices.
* [[Circles/Ede|Ede]]: a first school outreach at Baptist Practicing Primary School on 6 July 2026, with books, writing materials and welfare packs for teachers.
* [[Circles/Accra|Accra]]: monthly hands-on digital literacy sessions in April, May and June.
* Liberland: a riverbank and roadside clean-up in April 2026 that removed more than 35 bags of waste.

'''e-NABLE''' is a global network of volunteers who 3D print hands and arms for people born without fingers or hands, or who lost them, at little or no cost.

== What it does ==
A prosthetic hand from a clinic costs thousands, and a child outgrows one every year. e-NABLE hands are printed on ordinary desktop 3D printers and put together with cords and elastic. They strap to the forearm, and the fingers close when the wearer pulls on the cords.

The design files are free to download. A map lets someone who needs a hand find a volunteer nearby who owns a printer. That volunteer prints the hand, assembles it, fits it and gives it to the recipient, who pays nothing.

By its own count there are about 40,000 volunteers in over 100 countries, and an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 people have received a hand.

== Who runs it ==
* It began when the artist Ivan Owen made a large mechanical hand for a costume party and put the video online. A carpenter in South Africa who had lost his fingers got in touch.
* They built a hand for a five-year-old boy and put the design file online in January 2013.
* Professor Jon Schull then set up the community and the distribution map.
* Today it is a network of volunteers. Its fiscal sponsor is Rochester e-NABLE Limited, a 501(c)(3) corporation in Rochester, New York.

== Join or copy it ==
* If you need a hand, start at [https://enablingthefuture.org/learn-more-get-involved/ Learn more and get involved].

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669549000,"t":"edit","title":"Gapmap.uk","text":"{{Infobox project
| name     = gapmap.uk
| what     = A public map of concrete, fillable gaps in UK civic, economic and technological life
| run_by   = Logos Circle / London, with the site built and maintained by IP3 Studio
| status   = Active
| website  = https://gapmap.uk
| join     = Claim a "build now" gap, or suggest a new one at gapmap.uk/suggest
}}
'''gapmap.uk''' is the UK Gap Map: a list of what is missing in the UK, what would fill each gap, and who is building it. It is an initiative of [[Circles/London|Logos Circle / London]].

== What it does ==
* The map held 205 gaps across 18 domains when checked on 9 October 2026. One was in build and one had shipped.
* Every gap has a resolver category:
** '''Build now''' (55 gaps): no permission needed. A competent team could start today.
** '''Build together''' (42 gaps): needs a willing partner such as a council, an NHS body, a union or a regulator. No new law is needed.
** '''State-led''' (108 gaps): only the state can ship it. Evidence, prototypes and advocacy are still open to anyone.
* Each gap carries an urgency rank from 0 to 5, scored on importance, tractability, neglectedness and window. Each also has a horizon tag: short (0 to 2 years), mid (2 to 7 years) or long (7 years or more).
* Entries come from desk research against primary sources such as gov.uk, the ONS, the NAO, select committee reports and Law Commission papers. Each entry lists its sources and a review-by date.
* The about page calls the current map v3, based on a July 2026 research pass. Interviews with 30 to 50 practitioners are the next phase, before a public v1.0.

== Who runs it ==
* It is a Logos Circle / London initiative. IP3 Studio built the site and maintains it.
* LAN Issue 1 says it came out of twelve months of Circle meetings, smaller sessions and one-to-ones. Allies from the Anglofuturist movement took part.
* The Circle says the work followed a House of Lords debate on decentralised and centralised identity.
* It is modelled on gap-map.org by Convergent Research.

== Join or copy it ==
* Claim a gap with the site's 90-second wizard. You need no account, and the claim is posted publicly on GitHub.
* [https://gapmap.uk/suggest/ Suggest a gap], national or local. Suggestions are checked against primary sources before they appear.
* Correct an entry or discuss a gap on [https://github.com/Gap-Map-UK/uk-gap-map GitHub].
* Copy it for your own country or city. The site says the material is "free to use, free to copy, free to improve." The datasets (gaps.json, domains.json, graph.json) can be downloaded from the site. The repository does not name a licence.

{"v":1,"by":"ee7a5fc7ab70a820df10a4d3ba12f2e3f830c3f486b0d645eded9e8ff729ce08","ts":1791669551000,"t":"edit","title":"ΛPrize","text":"{{Infobox project | name = λPrize | what = Prizes for open-source work that fills gaps in the Logos stack | run_by = Logos Collective Association (Switzerland) | status = Active | licence = Winning work must be dual licensed MIT and Apache 2.0 | website = https://logos.co/lambda-prize | join = Build, get real users, then open a solution pull request at https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize }} The '''λPrize''' (Lambda Prize) is a [[Logos]] prize programme. It pays builders who independently make reusable open-source work for the Logos stack and show that others use it. The administrator is the Logos Collective Association, registered in Switzerland. The association sets the prizes, judges the claims and pays the winners. == How it works == # '''Pick a prize.''' Every prize is a file in the [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/tree/master/prizes prizes folder], named LP-XXXX. Each file sets out the success criteria, scope and prize amount. Most open prizes also have an Adoption section. # '''Build in public.''' Share your work on the Logos Discord, where #builder-hub is the main channel for builders. Look for people who will use it. The Logos Forum is the place for longer discussion. # '''Get real use.''' Each prize lists adoption evidence, such as real third-party use, on-chain activity, or human and social validation. # '''Claim it.''' Add a file to the solutions/ folder named after the prize, link your code, and open a pull request titled "Solution: LP-XXXX". Include the evidence for every adoption criterion. The reviewers will not take a headline number on trust. # '''Get paid.''' After your solution is merged, file the payment issue on GitHub. Prizes are paid in USDT on Ethereum. The first solution pull request that meets all the success and adoption criteria wins. A pull request is dated by when it was opened. Meeting the criteria without a pull request does not give you priority. There is one winner per prize unless the prize says otherwise. == The submission bar == Prizes are judged on a functionality gate plus adoption. Manual code review is not the main gate. The prize template sets these standard requirements, which each prize adapts: * No dependence on a central server. Use Logos Delivery for data and Logos Chat for peer-to-peer coordination. * A module or SDK other Logos modules can use. * A [[Basecamp]] app with local build instructions. * An interface description (IDL) for the LEZ program, made with the SPEL framework. * Deployed and tested on the LEZ devnet or testnet, with end-to-end tests in CI and CI green. * A README with deployment steps, program addresses and usage. * A demo script that works against a real local sequencer with RISC0_DEV_MODE=0, and a recorded video demo. * A FURPS self-assessment in the solution file. Reviewers clone the repository and run the demo script from a clean environment. It must work without changes. They may also ask questions to check who wrote the code. == Rules == * Up to 3 submissions per prize for each builder or team, and no more than one review a week. * First feedback is a simple pass or fail. * Code must be dual licensed under MIT and Apache 2.0. * Submissions are public. * Logos service providers and their contractors may not take part. They are also not counted towards adoption. * Logos has sole discretion over judging and awards. * To be paid you give your full legal name, country of residence and an Ethereum address. The address appears on the public GitHub issue, so the README suggests a single-use address if privacy matters. New prizes can only be proposed by Logos service providers for now. The README says a process for community ideas is planned. == Open prizes == Status as given in each prize file on 9 October 2026. {| class="wikitable" ! Prize !! Title !! Size !! Prize money !! Status |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0001.md LP-0001] || NFT Wallet Support and Private Ownership Proof || Medium || $5,000 || Open |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0018.md LP-0018] || OpenStreetMap integration: decentralised map data distribution || Medium || $1,500 || Open |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0021.md LP-0021] || LEZ Wallet and Provider SDK || X-Large || $20,000 || Open |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0023.md LP-0023] || LEZ Program Registry || Medium || $2,000 || Open |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0026.md LP-0026] || Forum App || Large || $5,500 || Open |} == Draft prizes == {| class="wikitable" ! Prize !! Title !! Size !! Prize money !! Status |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0022.md LP-0022] || Combined Blockchain and Zone Wallet || Large || $10,000 || Draft |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0004.md LP-0004] || Sealed-Bid Auction Using Shielded Balances || Large || To be decided || Draft, waiting for a LEZ timelock feature |- | [https://github.com/logos-co/lambda-prize/blob/master/prizes/LP-0011.md LP-0011] || Minimal Rust SDK for LEZ programs || Medium || To be decided || Draft, under review for overlap with the LEZ framework |} LP-0004 and LP-0011 appear in the prize files but not in the README table. == Closed prizes and winners == These prizes used an earlier build-and-review model and are closed to new entries. Several closed at 23:59 CEST on 11 September 2026. Entries to LP-0002, LP-0003 and LP-0008 received before that deadline are still being judged. '''[[Parallel polis]]''' is the idea that people living under an oppressive regime can build their own institutions alongside the official ones. The Czech dissident [[Václav Benda]] set it out in 1978 in an essay for the signatories of [[Charter 77]]. He proposed parallel structures in culture, education, information, the economy and politics, to supply what the official order failed to provide. The essay first circulated as [[samizdat]]. The Circles handbook traces its idea of a parallel society to the parallel polis, and the Logos website calls Logos "the private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies". '''[[Parallel polis]]''' is the idea that people living under an oppressive regime can build their own institutions alongside the official ones. The Czech dissident [[Václav Benda]] set it out in 1978 in an essay for the signatories of [[Charter 77]]. He proposed parallel structures in culture, education, information, the economy and politics, to supply what the official order failed to provide. The essay first circulated as [[samizdat]]. The Circles handbook traces its idea of a parallel society to the parallel polis, and the Logos website calls Logos "the private-by-default technology stack for parallel societies".
